verdict.headline: Iran set to unveil Hormuz deal Monday even as weekend tanker attack continued
verdict.label: S&P 500 closed the week at 7,656.98, down 0.6%; the 10Y yield ended Friday at 4.96%, its cycle high; WTI settled at $100.05 Friday; a tanker struck in the Strait of Hormuz Saturday killed one person and wounded four — the tanker war continued through the weekend even as Bloomberg reported Monday's Hormuz signing ceremony in Oman remains on track; September 16 FOMC hike priced at ~85.5%; BTC $76,853 Sunday
verdict.rationale_short:
The week closed with the S&P 500 down 0.6% at 7,656.98 after four losing sessions gave way to Friday's partial relief: stocks gained 0.86% as Iranian state media announced Tehran would meet Gulf states in Oman to discuss Hormuz transit, and crude fell 2.4% to a $100.05 settle. The week's driver was oil — WTI rose roughly 9.4% from Monday's open as US-Iran military exchanges in the Strait of Hormuz cut tanker traffic at the world's most-used energy shipping chokepoint to a fraction of normal. Two data releases compounded the read on Friday: August core CPI rose 0.3% against a 0.2% estimate, with the shelter index — roughly a third of core and not an energy line — jumping to 0.3% after two consecutive months at 0.1%; and preliminary September consumer sentiment fell to 47.8, the second-lowest reading since 1952, with year-ahead inflation expectations jumping to 4.6% from 4.0%. The ten-year yield closed Friday at 4.96%, four basis points from 5.00%, its highest of this rate cycle.

The weekend produced a new data point. An Iranian commercial container ship was struck near Hengam Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday — one person killed, four wounded, according to Iranian state media, confirmed by UKMTO. Iran also separately claimed a strike on a US-linked vessel; the US has operated under a "tanker for tanker" retaliatory policy since early September. These attacks came a day after Friday's diplomatic signal — the tanker war and the Oman diplomatic track are running simultaneously, not sequentially. Bloomberg reported Sunday that the Iran-GCC signing ceremony in Muscat is still on for Monday despite the weekend attack, with Iran set to formally unveil its temporary shipping lane arrangement to Gulf states. But Saudi Arabia submitted amendments over concerns the deal could establish a new status quo in the waterway, and Bahrain said it would not attend. The United States is not at the table.

The week ahead concentrates three catalysts, and their order matters. Monday's Oman outcome is the first read: a signed, Saudi-inclusive framework before Wednesday takes the energy shock out of October CPI data and changes the framing of the FOMC hike from an emergency response to a planned cycle step. A ceremony that Bahrain boycotts and Saudi conditions are unresolved does not do the same work even if a document is signed — crude's Monday settle is the real-time judgment. Wednesday then concentrates August retail sales (consensus roughly 0.2% against July's 0.5%, at 8:30 a.m. ET) alongside the FOMC decision and updated dot plot (2:00 p.m. ET). A 25-basis-point move to 3.75%-4.00% is priced at roughly 85.5%; the dot plot's median projection for the rate path beyond September is the market-moving element. A dot showing two or more additional hikes past September, delivered into a ten-year that is four basis points from 5.00% and a thirty-year that is eight from the 2007 peak of 5.44%, would reprice the long end in the same session. A dot showing September as the final move, paired with crude below $100 from an Oman deal, says the opposite.

Eurasia Group has moved its Hormuz de-escalation timeline to year-end; Iran's stated posture through September has been to widen the conflict rather than wind it down. A deal that is signed while attacks continue, with Bahrain absent and Saudi conditions unresolved, is a different object from the framework the Friday relief rally priced. The gap between what is signed Monday and what is enforced in the lane is what oil prices will trade this week.
verdict.lede_short: The S&P 500 closed the week down 0.6% at 7,656.98 as oil rose 9.4% on Hormuz hostilities and August core CPI ran a tenth hot; the 10Y yield hit 4.96%, four basis points from its cycle trigger at 5.00%. The weekend added a new development: a tanker was struck near Hengam Island on Saturday — one dead, four wounded — while Bloomberg reported Monday's Iran-GCC signing ceremony in Oman is still on track. Wednesday concentrates retail sales and the FOMC decision and dot plot in the same session, with a 25 bp hike to 3.75%-4.00% priced at 85.5%.

trade_setups.asset: Hormuz signing ceremony — Iran-GCC ministers in Oman, Monday September 14
trade_setups.thesis: Iran is set to formally unveil its Hormuz shipping arrangement to Gulf states in Muscat on Monday. Bloomberg reported Sunday the ceremony is on track despite Saturday's tanker attack. The agreement establishes a temporary joint Iran-Oman lane through the strait, to be notified to the IMO. Saudi Arabia submitted amendments and Bahrain will not attend — the deal's effect on actual vessel routing depends on whether amendments are resolved and whether all key Gulf states participate. A signed framework with Saudi acceptance and a reduction in attacks before Wednesday changes the framing of the FOMC hike from emergency oil-shock response to planned cycle step, removes the energy input from October CPI, and could take WTI sharply below $100. A ceremony that proceeds with Bahrain absent and Saudi conditions unresolved carries less force even if a document is signed.
trade_setups.entry: WTI's Monday settle is the observable: a first close below $100 since the conflict began signals either a framework took hold or the oil premium is unwinding. A close above $102 — above Friday's opening level before the Oman announcement — signals talks stalled or a new incident has occurred. A close between $100 and $102 says neither has resolved.
trade_setups.invalidation: A new Hormuz attack on Monday morning before talks begin, or a statement from Iran that it will not reduce patrols regardless of what is signed, would push crude above $102 and set up the committee to hike into an unresolved supply shock.

trade_setups.asset: Federal Reserve dot plot — September 16, 2:00 p.m. ET
trade_setups.thesis: A 25-basis-point hike to 3.75%-4.00% is priced at roughly 85.5%. The rate move is not the read — the Summary of Economic Projections is. A dot plot showing two or more additional hikes past September pushes the ten-year (4 bps from 5.00%) and the thirty-year (8 bps from the 2007 peak of 5.44%) toward their formal trigger levels. A dot showing September as the final move, especially if paired with a Monday crude signal below $100, compresses the long end and changes the week's framing from further tightening to near-cycle-end. The June SEP had the median member projecting 3.75%-4.00% at year-end — a single hike from the July hold. If the September SEP moves that median to 4.00%-4.25% or higher, the committee sees more than one additional move from here.
trade_setups.entry: 5.00% on the ten-year and 5.44% on the thirty-year are the upside levels. A post-decision ten-year rally back below 4.90% would indicate the market reads the hike as a cycle end rather than a pause.
trade_setups.invalidation: A hold rather than a hike — priced at roughly 14.5% — would move the market in a direction different from any current consensus and would require explanation in the press conference.
trade_setups.horizon: Wednesday September 16, 2:00 p.m. ET into Thursday

trade_setups.asset: August retail sales — Wednesday September 16, 8:30 a.m. ET
trade_setups.thesis: Retail sales for August print two hours before equity markets open and ninety minutes before the FOMC statement, creating the first live read on the growth side of the trade-off in the same session as the rate decision. Consensus is roughly 0.2% against July's 0.5%. Higher gasoline prices may flatter the headline while real spending falls. A weak print below 0.2% puts slowing consumer spending alongside a hike into an oil shock — the conflict between the two halves of the Fed's mandate made visible in one morning's data. Core retail excluding autos, gas, and food strips the gasoline effect and is the version to watch if the headline surprises.
trade_setups.entry: 0.2% is consensus; anything below 0.0% says the gasoline tax is reaching spending and begins to build a case that the oil shock is weakening demand, not just raising prices. Anything at or above 0.5% — matching July — removes the dovish growth framing from the session.
trade_setups.invalidation: An in-line 0.2% print with normal revisions to July leaves Wednesday entirely in the dot plot's hands; neither side of the growth-versus-inflation tension is confirmed by the data.
